topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: An API communicates what callers may depend on; an ABI describes how compiled components interact. A source-compatible change can still break an old binary, and a stable-looking class name does not guarantee a stable layout. Harbor’s accumulator uses Pimpl to hide implementation storage while keeping its move and failure behavior explicit.

topics.title: 20.1.1 Minimizing Coupling
topics.summary: Expose the operations and domain types consumers need, not every implementation detail available. A smaller public surface reduces the number of assumptions that later changes can violate. Avoid leaking third-party containers or platform handles unless they are intentionally part of the contract.

topics.title: 20.1.2 Preserving Encapsulation
topics.summary: Encapsulation protects invariants by controlling how state changes. It does not mean hiding all information from tests; expose meaningful observations that let callers verify behavior without depending on internal representation. A count and total can be stable observations even when the storage strategy changes.

This can reduce header dependencies and hide layout details of the implementation. The public object’s own representation and special-member behavior still require a compatibility policy.

topics.title: 20.2.1 Understanding ABI Concerns
topics.summary: ABI compatibility can depend on compiler family, standard-library implementation, runtime settings, calling convention, exception model, symbol names, and public type layout. Rebuilding every component together tests source integration, not compatibility with already-shipped consumers.

topics.title: 20.2.2 Applying the Pimpl Idiom
topics.summary: A unique_ptr to an incomplete Impl can appear in a public header, but destruction and relevant special members should be defined where Impl is complete. This avoids requiring clients to instantiate deletion against an incomplete type. Move operations also need a stated moved-from policy.
